newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: BIS adds nine new members to expand global role.
newsitem.headline: BIS adds nine new members to expand global role.

text.p: The Bank for International Settlements (BIS), central bank to the worlds' central banks, on Monday said it would invite nine major new central banks across the world to join its ranks as it seeks to play a more global role.

Wim Duisenberg, chairman and president of BIS, the world's oldest international financial institution, told a news conference the central banks of Brazil, Mexico, China, Hong Kong, Singapore, India, South Korea, Russia and Saudi Arabia had been invited to join the BIS.
BIS and the new members have already been in talks over membership over several years and Duisenberg said he assumed all the invited banks would join by March 1997 at the latest.

BIS was founded in 1930 to deal with the settlement of German reparations after World War One, but always played a crucial role as a centre for cooperation among the world's most influential central banks through times of crises and wars.

Duisenberg, who is also president of the Dutch central bank, said the expansion of membership -- the first increase in BIS shareholders in 25 years -- would not threaten the BIS' role as a centre for central bank cooperation.
"We certainly don't want to become a second IMF," Duisenberg said, noting the new members have increasingly participated in BIS activities over the last decade.
"It is a goal to let the BIS play a more global role than it has in the past," Duisenberg said.

Selection of new members was based on representative economic and financial criteria as well as the central banks' involvement in, and contribution to, internatioal economic cooperation, Duisenberg said.
Seven of the nine new members represent the largest economies in their region and Hong Kong and Singapore are home to major financial markets.

To become members in the exclusive club for the world's most powerful central banks, the central banks will purchase an undisclosed number of BIS shares that are not held by its other 32 members, only five of which are not European.

In addition to providing a forum for central bank cooperation, BIS also provides a range of banking services to its members and is a focal point for research into international monetary and financial issues.

But it is as gathering point -- a home-away-from-home -- for central bank governors that gives BIS a unique standing among other international institutions, such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
The board of the BIS is made up of the Group of 10 (G10)central banks and its expansion will not change the G10's role as the core of BIS.
Ten times a year G10 central bank governors travel to BIS' headquarters in Basle to huddle and discuss the latest economic and financial developments that are changing the world.
G10 comprise the United States, Canada, Japan, Germany, France, Britain, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, Sweden, Switzerland.

These monthly meetings, which are informal and confidential, have helped develop an atmosphere of trust among central bankers so they can pick up a telephone and consult each other to reach a coordinated response in times of financial crises.
